guide.title: Unit 7: Complexity, qualification, and sentences: review guide
guide.intro: Complex issues need arguments that account for tensions and limits. This unit practices recognizing complexity, qualifying claims with words, phrases, and clauses, responding to counterarguments, and building sentences whose structure shows how ideas relate.

sections.title: Complexity
body: An issue is complex when reasonable people weigh competing values (freedom and safety, cost and benefit) or when the facts vary by situation. Sophisticated arguments acknowledge these tensions rather than pretending they don't exist.
Introductions and conclusions can signal complexity: an introduction might present a genuine dilemma, and a conclusion might explain when the writer's position applies.
points: Ask: under what conditions would the opposite be true?
Complexity isn't indecision; the writer still takes a position.

sections.title: Qualifying claims and addressing counterarguments
body: Words (often, some), phrases (in most cases), and clauses (unless the cost rises) limit a claim's scope. A concession grants part of an opposing view; a rebuttal explains why the writer's position still holds.
Qualifying is not weakening: a claim the evidence fully supports is stronger than an absolute one a single example could refute.

sections.title: Sentence development, clauses, and conventions
body: Independent clauses can stand alone; dependent clauses (beginning with although, because, when, which) cannot. Placing an idea in the main clause emphasizes it; placing it in a dependent clause subordinates it.

Conventions of punctuation make these relationships clear: a semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses, a colon introduces an explanation or list, and commas set off introductory dependent clauses.
points: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses (a comma splice).
Parallel structure clarifies lists and comparisons.

example.prompt: Combine to emphasize the benefit: “The program is expensive.” “It saves lives.”
example.solution: “Although the program is expensive, it saves lives.” The cost goes in the dependent clause; the benefit gets the emphasis of the main clause.

misconceptions: “Qualifying a claim means you aren't sure.”
It means the claim is precise about what the evidence shows.
It joins independent clauses or separates complex list items.
Addressing them makes an argument more credible.
Sentence structure should fit the relationship between ideas.

passages.title: Passage 1: The homework question
text: (1) Few school debates generate as much heat as homework. Parents who remember long evenings at the kitchen table are sure it builds discipline; students who spend those evenings exhausted are sure it does not.

(2) The research suggests that both are partly right. For older students, a moderate amount of homework is generally associated with better achievement, although the benefit appears to level off as the hours climb. For young children, evidence of any academic benefit is much weaker.

(3) Admittedly, homework can teach habits that tests do not measure. Yet a habit learned at the cost of sleep and family time may not be worth teaching. The better question is not whether to assign homework but how much, to whom, and for what purpose.
passages.attribution: Written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes research on homework in general terms rather than quoting a specific study.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Passage 2: Should we stop changing the clocks?
text: (1) Twice a year, most of the country moves its clocks, and twice a year people complain. The complaint is easy; the solution is not.

(2) Permanent standard time would give brighter winter mornings, which some sleep scientists favor because morning light helps set the body's clock. Permanent daylight saving time would give brighter winter evenings, which many businesses favor because shoppers stay out later.
(3) Each choice trades one kind of light for another. Unless lawmakers decide which they value more, health or commerce, ending the clock change will simply replace one complaint with another.
passages.attribution: Written for StudySprint by its editors. It describes the debate in general terms.

passages.title: Draft 1: A student paragraph about a skate park
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph. It may need revision.

(1) The town should build a skate park. (2) Skateboarders currently use the library steps, this damages the stone and annoys patrons. (3) A skate park would cost money. (4) It would give skaters a safe place. (5) It would protect public property. (6) It would bring visitors to town.
passages.attribution: Written for StudySprint by its editors.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Draft 2: A student introduction about a four-way stop
text: The following is a draft introduction to a student's letter to the town traffic committee. It may need revision.
(1) The intersection of Oak and Third is dangerous. (2) A traffic light would solve all of its problems. (3) Last year there were six collisions there. (4) The committee should install a light.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?
choices: To state the writer's final position
To describe the writer's own childhood
To provide research evidence
To present the opposing views that make the homework debate heated
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 lays out parents' and students' opposing certainties.
choiceExplanations: The writer doesn't describe their own childhood.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 2, the clause “although the benefit appears to level off as the hours climb” serves to
choices: describe young children's homework
introduce a story
limit the claim about homework's benefit for older students
contradict the claim that homework helps older students
questions.explanation: The clause qualifies the benefit: it exists, but more hours don't keep adding to it.
choiceExplanations: Young children are discussed in the next sentence.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 respond to the view that homework builds discipline?
choices: It ignores the view
It rejects the view without explanation
It concedes that homework may teach habits, then argues that the cost may outweigh that benefit
It accepts the view completely
questions.explanation: “Admittedly” grants the point; “Yet” introduces the rebuttal about sleep and family time.

questions.prompt: The final sentence reframes the debate. What does this reframing accomplish?
choices: It introduces a new topic unrelated to homework
It shows that the writer agrees with the parents
It ends the essay without a position
It replaces an all-or-nothing question with one that accounts for the complexity the research reveals
questions.explanation: Asking “how much, to whom, and for what purpose” reflects the evidence that homework's value depends on age and amount.
choiceExplanations: The writer partly agrees with both sides.
The reframing is the writer's position.

questions.prompt: What makes the issue in the passage complex, according to the writer?
choices: Scientists and businesses agree
Each option benefits one set of values at the expense of another
The clocks are expensive to change
No one complains about changing clocks
questions.explanation: Morning light serves health; evening light serves commerce. Choosing one sacrifices the other.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, the semicolon in “The complaint is easy; the solution is not” serves to
choices: set off a dependent clause
join two closely related, contrasting independent clauses
introduce a list
mark a quotation
questions.explanation: The two short clauses balance each other, emphasizing the contrast.

questions.prompt: Paragraph 2 uses two sentences with the same structure. What is the effect of this parallel structure?
choices: It makes the two options easy to compare point by point
It makes the paragraph harder to follow
It shows that the options are identical
It hides the writer's opinion
questions.explanation: Matching structure (“Permanent … would give …, which … favor because …”) lines up the options for comparison.
choiceExplanations: It makes the paragraph easier to follow.
They differ; the structure highlights how.
The structure supports comparison, not concealment.

questions.prompt: In the final sentence, how does the clause beginning “Unless lawmakers decide…” shape the writer's claim?
choices: It introduces a counterargument the writer rejects
It sets the condition under which ending the clock change would succeed
It shows the writer supports permanent daylight saving time
It states that lawmakers will never decide
questions.explanation: The conditional clause limits the claim: ending the change only solves the problem if a value choice is made.
choiceExplanations: The writer doesn't pick an option.
It describes a condition, not a prediction.

questions.prompt: Sentence (2) contains an error. Which revision is correct?
choices: Skateboarders, currently use the library steps, this damages the stone, and annoys patrons.
Skateboarders currently use the library steps, this damages, the stone and annoys patrons.
Skateboarders currently use the library steps; this damages the stone and annoys patrons.
Skateboarders currently use the library steps this damages the stone and annoys patrons.
questions.explanation: The original joins two independent clauses with only a comma (a comma splice). A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
choiceExplanations: This adds incorrect commas and keeps the splice.
This keeps the comma splice and adds an error.

questions.prompt: The writer wants to combine sentences (3) and (4) so that the benefit receives the emphasis. Which is best?
choices: A skate park would cost money; it would cost money.
Although a skate park would give skaters a safe place, it would cost money.
Although a skate park would cost money, it would give skaters a safe place.
A skate park would cost money and give skaters a safe place.
questions.explanation: Putting the cost in the dependent clause and the benefit in the main clause emphasizes the benefit.
choiceExplanations: This puts the benefit in the dependent clause and the cost in the main clause, so the cost gets the emphasis.
“And” treats cost and benefit as equal.

questions.prompt: Which revision best combines sentences (4), (5), and (6) using parallel structure?
choices: It would give skaters a safe place, protect public property, and bring visitors to town.
It would give skaters a safe place, protecting public property, and visitors would come.
It would give skaters a safe place and property and visitors.
Giving skaters a safe place, it protects property and also visitors.
questions.explanation: Three verb phrases in the same form (give, protect, bring) make a clear, parallel list.
choiceExplanations: This drops the verbs and changes the meaning.

questions.prompt: Sentence (3) mentions a counterargument but doesn't respond to it. Which revision best concedes and rebuts?
choices: Money doesn't matter.
A skate park would cost money, but the town already spends money every year repairing the library steps.
A skate park would cost a lot of money.
Some people don't like skateboarding.
questions.explanation: It grants the cost, then rebuts it with a comparison to an existing expense.
choiceExplanations: This dismisses the concern without a reason.
This raises a different objection without answering it.

choices: Sentence (1)
Sentence (3)
Sentence (4)
Sentence (2)

questions.prompt: Which revision of sentence (2) best qualifies the claim?
choices: A traffic light would solve every problem in town.
A traffic light might do something.
A traffic light is a light.
A traffic light would likely reduce collisions by giving each direction a clear turn.
questions.explanation: “Likely reduce” and the explanation make a precise, defensible claim.
choiceExplanations: This is too vague to argue anything.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would best open the introduction for the traffic committee?
choices: Six collisions in a single year have made the four-way stop at Oak and Third the town's most dangerous intersection.
Traffic exists in every town.
Cars were invented over a century ago.
I like to walk.
questions.explanation: It establishes the exigence with specific evidence the committee cares about.
choiceExplanations: This is irrelevant to the committee.

questions.prompt: The committee might note that traffic lights can increase rear-end crashes. How could the writer best account for this complexity?
choices: Acknowledge the trade-off and argue that, at this intersection, preventing the more serious side-impact collisions matters more
Ignore it so the letter stays short
Say that rear-end crashes never happen
Withdraw the request
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the trade-off and explaining why the benefit outweighs it here keeps the argument credible.
choiceExplanations: Ignoring a known objection weakens credibility.
This is false and easy to refute.
One trade-off doesn't require abandoning the position.
